It is certain that before 1380/1381, Rosenberg was not a fief but allodial property. Which of the Uissigheim-Rosenbergs acquired it cannot be said with final certainty. As already mentioned, there is some evidence for Eberhard Rufus. The period must have been the 1270s, which points to an era in which a major power shift had begun in the "Hinterer Odenwald" and the Bauland. The holders of power, the free nobles of Dürn, were in a state of decline⁶⁵. The main beneficiaries were Mainz and Würzburg. In such a shift, it is easy to overlook that the ministerials could also very well profit from the weakness of their lords. There were ministerial families who were drawn into the vortex of the Dürn sell-off, and there were others, like the Rüdt, who benefited from it. Unfortunately, the state of the sources does not permit the assertion that the extinction of the free nobles of Uissigheim opened up similar opportunities for advancement for their ministerials of the same name as it did for the Rüdt. Nevertheless, a certain probability may be assumed.  65 Werner Eichhorn: The Lordship of Dürn and its Development until the End of the Hohenstaufen. 1966. Peter Paul Albert: The Noble Lords of Dürn (Between Neckar and Main 15, 1936).

The expansion of Eberhard Rufus from the Tauber region must be seen in the context of the decline of the Dürn family. It is unlikely that the castle in Rosenberg did not yet exist and that he was the one who built it. This is contradicted by a frequently observed finding. Place names of the \-berg/-burg type belong to the period of high medieval castle foundations in the 11th/12th centuries⁶⁶. Now, the sparse remains of a 7th-century row grave field have been found on the outskirts of Rosenberg⁶⁷. The associated settlement cannot possibly have already had the name that is to be assigned to the high medieval set of names. Two conclusions arise from this: At the time Eberhard Rufus established himself here, a Rosenberg Castle, whose name was transferred to the surrounding settlement, already existed. Eberhard Rufus can therefore not be considered its builder.  66 Hans Martin Maurer: The Origin of the High Medieval Noble Castle in Southwestern Germany. In: ZGO 117 (1969) pp. 295-322. Adolf Bach: German Onomastics Vol. II/2 1954) pp. 355 and 382.  67 Robert Koch: Archaeological Finds of the Migration Period from the Main-Tauber Area (Germanic Monuments of the Migration Period Series A Vol. 8, 1967) pp. 193ff.

Therefore, one must assume—the conclusion is compelling—that there was a noble family that made way for him in some manner. It is conceivable that the Dürn themselves sold one of their castles to Eberhard Rufus. This would explain the allodial character of Rosenberg. However, it is equally possible that one of the Dürn's ministerial families was the seller. There are examples where the Dürn released ministerials from their feudal obligations and permitted the sale of the fief⁶⁸.  68 On 24. 10. 1284, Boppo II of Dürn-Dilsberg permitted the debt-ridden Hartwig von Ernstein to sell properties that were fiefs; WUB 10 No. 3573, p. 103. Similarly, Rupert III of Dürn-Forchtenberg in 1321 for Ludwig von Heineberg: StA Ludwigsburg B 503 Doc. 629.

There is some evidence for this second possibility, although it must be admitted that conclusive proof cannot be provided. In the year 1251, Konrad von Dürn carried out a division of inheritance⁶⁹. Following the counts and free nobles, the witness list names a Monachus de Rosenberg. He was a Dürn ministerial, which is further confirmed by a document issued by Boppo I of Dürn in 1253. It was witnessed by Conradus dictus monachus de Roseberg (Conrad called monk of Rosenberg)⁷⁰. Some other pieces of evidence: Conradus monachus endowed an anniversary mass in 1255⁷¹; in 1261, Monachus de Rosenberg and his descendants transferred possessions to Bronnbach Abbey⁷². He died soon after, because in 1270 his widow (relicta) Elisabeth stipulated that after her death a farm in Seckach should go to the nunnery of Seligental73. Ludwig Monachus and his younger brother Konrad, probably sons of Elisabeth, were among the sellers of Stolzeneck Castle in the Neckar Valley to Elector Palatine Ludwig in 1284, whom both called their lord74.  69 WUB 4 No. 1181, pp. 249 ff.  70 WUB 5 No. 1264, pp. 27 ff.  71 Friedrich von Weech: Palatinate Regesta. In: ZGO 24 (1872) pp. 269-327, here: p. 297.  72 StA Wertheim Lit. A 426 fol. 65.  73 F. V. v. Gudenus (as in note 16) No. 17, p. 686; in 1269 Conrad Monachus had confirmed the anniversary endowment; cf. F. von Weech (as in note 71) p. 297.  74 Franz Joseph Mone: The Neckar Valley from Heidelberg to Wimpfen. In: ZGO 11 (1860) pp. 39-72, here: pp. 65f. Apparently, the castle belonged to the County of Dilsberg, which the Palatinate acquired from the Dürn. This in turn confirms the original affiliation of the Mönch family to the Dürn's ministerials.

The Mönch von Rosenberg family has not been easy to classify so far⁷⁵. Some wanted to see them as members of the lower noble family von Pülfringen or as a side branch of the Uissigheim-Rosenbergs⁷⁶. In all probability, they are an independent noble family and the original owners of Rosenberg castle and village. There is no connection to our Uissigheim-Rosenbergs, as their coats of arms are also completely different⁷⁷.  75 On the Mönch family, only F. Dambacher: The Monks of Rosenberg. In: ZGO 10 (1859) pp. 123-128; J. Kindler von Knobloch-O. Frh. von Stotzingen: Upper Baden Book of Lineages Vol. 3 (1919) pp. 153 and 161.  76 Franz Gehrig argued for a connection with the Pülfringen family in: The Knightly Family of Pülfringen. In: Rhein-Neckar-Zeitung 5. 10. 1982. Cf. StA Wertheim Lit. A 436 fol. 9: Conradus cognomine monachus advocatus Wimpinen(sis) de Bilversheim (Conrad, surnamed monk, advocate of Wimpfen, of Bilversheim), but there are quite a number of noble families where this cognomen appears.  77 An upright monk, holding three flowers or a rose in his outstretched hands.

Insofar as their possessions are transmitted through the fief books of the prince-bishopric, they are grouped, like those of the Uissigheim-Rosenbergs, around the eponymous castle: Under Bishop Andreas von Gundelfingen, Monachus de Rosenberg was enfeoffed with the patronage and tithe in Adelsheim, and Cünradus dictus Munch with half the tithe there⁷⁸; from Bishop Otto von Wolfskeel (1335-1345), Lud. Munch de Rosenberg miles received half the Adelsheim tithe, the tithe of Höpfingen, two parts of the great and small tithe of Gies and Bronnacker (here by half), and two parts of that of Niederzimmern⁷⁹. In 1349, Lutzo dictus Munich de Rosemberg was enfeoffed with half the Adelsheim tithe, 2 parts of the tithe in Niederzimmern, 2 parts of the great tithe of Gies and Ensigheim, among others⁸⁰.  78 H. Hoffmann (as in note 36) No. 10, p. 33 and 744, p. 87.  79 Ibid., No. 3969, p. 389.  80 H*. Hoffmann:* The Fief Book of the Prince-Bishops Albrecht von Hohenlohe (Sources and Research 33, 1983) No. 731, p. 87.

As far as can be gathered from the Würzburg fief records, at the beginning of the 14th century the Mönch family had already departed from Rosenberg and found themselves relegated to peripheral possessions. The appurtenances of Rosenberg Castle likely included the neighboring settlements of Bronnacker, Gies, and Ensigheim⁸¹. These are also later found in the hands of the Uissigheim-Rosenbergs. Towards the end of the 15th century, the Mönch family gave up their last possessions in the Bauland. This family died out in 1679 with Peter Mönch, Vogt of Isenburg (near Horb)⁸².  81 Cf. Albert Krieger: Topographical Dictionary of the Grand Duchy of Baden Vol. 1 (1905) col. 519 and 716. Gies is located in the district of Osterburken, Ensigheim in that of Rosenberg. 82 J. Kindler von Knobloch-O. Frh. von Stotzingen (as in note 75) p. 161.

If one accepts the succession of ownership from Mönch to Uissigheim-Rosenberg as a given, the question arises as to how the change took place. Eberhard Rufus probably bought the castle and village, which would indicate the economic distress of the Mönch family. They were not alone in this within the Dürn's ministerialage.

It must be admitted that some of these considerations are somewhat uncertain. However, they offer a plausible explanation for movements of property and lordship that have hitherto received little attention.

An attempt was made to expand or at least to specify some details of the state of knowledge on the early history of the Rosenbergs since H. Bauer.  1. The thesis, assumed by H. Bauer and substantiated by W. Möller, of an identity between the Uissigheimers and the Rosenbergs is confirmed.  2. A distinction must be made between the high noble family of Uissigheim, which died out in the mid-13th century, and the lower nobles of the same name. The latter become tangible in 1260 and probably originally belonged to the ministerialage of the free or high nobles.  3. Who the descendants of the brothers Eberhard and Arnold were remains hypothetical, as does the progeny of some other Uissigheimers belonging to this generation.  4. In the second half of the 13th century, four to five family branches can be expected, whose genealogical connection is partly unclear.  5. With Eberhard Rufus and the children of Arnold von Uissigheim, it was possible to extend the Rosenberg family tree backwards by one generation.  6. With them begins the division of the Uissigheimers into two main branches, one of which continued the old name, while the other took up that of Rosenberg Castle.  7. The background of this acquisition is the decline of the free nobles of Dürn.  8. The family tree created by W. Möller, which was based on the distinction between an "older (Eberhardian)" main line and an "Arnoldian" one, can possibly be corrected to the effect that there were two main lines \- an older one descending from Eberhard Rufus, and a younger one that split with Eberhard III (II) and Arnold I, but inherited from the former. All subsequent Lords of Rosenberg descend from it.  9. A prerequisite for belonging to the top group of the Franconian lower nobility, and thus also for having extraordinary financial means, was service to the powerful. The biography of Eberhard III (II) serves as an illustration of this.  10. Based on the name and the property situation, the Mönch family, who were not a side branch of the Uissigheim-Rosenbergs, are to be considered the former owners of the castle and village. The change of ownership is to be dated to the years before 1285.  11. The castle and village were acquired as allodial property. Their conversion into a fief is connected with the purchase of the Boxberg commandery in 1381.
